newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Grain - Crop good, politics hazy.
newsitem.headline: Australian Grain - Crop good, politics hazy.

text.p: The Australian grains focus shifted last week to the Canberra Convention Centre where predictions emerged of another sizeable Australian wheat crop and sharp words showed just how greatly Australia, the U.S. and the EU disagree on the way wheat should be sold to the world.
Trevor Flugge, chairman of the Australian Wheat Board (AWB), put the size of Australia's 1997/98 wheat crop at a minimum of 17 million tonnes with the possibility of 20 million tonnes.

Official forecasting agency, the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE), which hosted the Outlook '97 conference, was slightly more conservative, forecasting the next wheat crop at 16.98 million tonnes, down from the current record crop of 23.12 million.
The trade agrees with estimates in this range. Bill Mitchell of New England Agricultural Traders said present moisture was very good and a crop of 17-20 million tonnes was seen.

Flugge's conference estimate of an opening 1997/98 wheat pool price of A$170-A$180 would not have an impact on area planted, with the potential good for the pool price to rise to current pool price levels of A$192 a tonne, he said.

Behind the wash of figures at the ABARE conference, Flugge and Jim Parker, assistant administrator foreign agricultural service of the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), clashed sharply over what the Australian industry sees as the key to the success of its marketing programme.
Parker criticised the AWB's monopoly export powers as "manipulative" and said they would be challenged before the next round of the GATT.
Flugge told reporters later that Parker's position was "nonsense". "They can't compete with us, they're in danger of becoming a residual player in the world market," he said.
Flugge sees the disagreement dragging on for so many years in the World Trade Organisation that last week he treated the issue as almost background noise.
The U.S. export enhancement programme (EEP) more greatly distorted world markets than the AWB's export monopoly, he said.
Parker's further criticism, of European Union (EU) agricultural export subsidies, was in turn opposed by EU agricultural commissioner Franz Fischler.
Fischler disputed Parker's calculation that Europe would spend US$10 billion this year on commodities subsidies against a U.S. Congress export subsidy appropriation of $100 million.
No specific amount had been set aside, said Fischler, who then side-stepped questions on whether EU grains export subsidies were likely to increase this year.
The apparent wrap-up on the politics of grains from the week's meetings: business as usual for Australia, the U.S. and the EU as major players in the world grains trade.
Australian grains prices continued to rise last week in defiance of the downtrend in the U.S.
Sorghum added about A$1 a tonne to about A$156 Newcastle in light trading, while barley firmed up to A$5 a tonne to between A$115 and A$130 a tonne, Mitchell said.
The AWB's pool price boost of A$4 to A$192 surprised the trade in view of Chicago prices. But AWB exports at good prices indicated the pool price rise was justified, he said.

Wheat futures held up well over the past week with settlement prices for near-term contracts of March, May and July 1997 rising between A$4 and A$9 a tonne and more distant contracts edging back by A$1-A$2 a tonne over the week.
